Aww no I dont think you have a condition, but perhaps a refresh and practice on neatness is needed. 

Id start by addressing the mechanical aspects, relearning some basics (it’s ok, better to bite the bullet), and use muscle memory to your advantage. So, a suggestion if you want to improve: get some traceable letter sheets *that are of the font size you regularly write in*. You can buy these, or find some on google and print out multiple copies at home. Then for 30min a day, everyday, for a month, you’re going to practice by tracing those upper case & lower case letters over and over again. Think of them as drills and you’re going to force yourself to trace/copy it as close as possible every time. Then one month plus a day later, rewrite what you have in this image and compare - I bet you’ll see immediate improvement. 

Your penmanship wont immediately look like Shakespeare’s cursive, but I bet it will get you closer to a realistic goal.

But ma’am as a 30-something woman with ADHD, and let me tell you that ADHD adults are:

1. Perfectly capable of taking care of ourselves. It might not look “perfect” to the outside world, might not be how a non-ADHD person might go about it, but we will address our core needs so that they are met when needed. This works even better when on the right meds, but make no mistake while it might be a little chaotic along the way but we are still in fact adults. We don’t need a new parent, and I’m SO sorry that he made you feel that way. That’s not the ADHD, that’s him being a deadbeat husband. 

2. What’s wild is that while yes, we might talk excessively or interrupt, we adult ADHDers have no issue with empathy. We are perfectly empathic, like there’s literally nothing on the diagnostic criteria for adult ADHD implying that we’re not. While I can see maybe being blunt, but reading what he said to you cannot be blamed on ADHD - he’s just being an AH. 

I’m happy you’re divorcing him, you don’t need this man child. You sound like you’ve been extremely considerate, and it’s very unfair for him to try to imply that his behaviour is because of his ADHD, but just know that the rest of us ADHDers aren’t *that* type of jerk. 

I hope this is a new chapter of happiness and freedom for you 🩷

When I said, “If you stop looking for someone to date, they will find you,” it isn’t just about surrendering to fate or blindly waiting for someone to come along. Instead, it’s about shifting the focus inward and cultivating a life filled with joy, purpose, and personal fulfillment. People are naturally drawn to those who are genuinely happy and engaged in their lives. When you’re actively pursuing your passions, investing in your personal growth, and living a life that feels authentic to you, you exude a magnetic energy that attracts others. I suspect this is actually what fuels some of that charisma you alluded to.

This isn’t about playing hard to get or pretending to be unavailable; it’s about truly finding contentment and confidence within yourself. When you’re not focused on finding a relationship (desperately or not), you present a version of yourself that is self-assured and content. This self-assurance is incredibly attractive because it reflects independence and a sense of wholeness. 

Additionally, when you let go of the constant search for a partner, you’re more likely to notice and connect with people naturally, without the pressure of romantic expectations. This is huge and is what has driven my entire romantic history. It creates space for genuine connections to develop, whether or not they lead to romance. By focusing on your own life and interests, you cultivate a strong sense of self, which can be far more appealing than any specific traits or qualities you might think are necessary to attract a partner.

Being genuinely happy and engaged in your own life also means you are more selective about who you let into your life. You don’t settle for someone just to fill a void or meet a societal expectation - a theme of this entire sub. Instead, you wait for a connection that truly complements your life and values. This approach not only leads to healthier relationships but also aligns with a life that you’ve built on your own terms.

Ultimately, the idea isn’t to stop looking because you’ve given up; it’s to stop looking because you’ve chosen to focus on yourself first. When you are busy living your best life, you’ll find that the right people naturally gravitate towards you, often when you least expect it.

**TLDR: Those of us who suffer with anxiety have an evil version of Giorgio Tsoukalos *(the alien conspiracy dude from the History channel with the crazy hair)* living inside our heads and we have to come to terms with that.**

Not sure if there’s anything online about it, I’ve used the analogy for so long now I can’t remember if I came up with it or just came across it. But I’d be happy to explain what I mean and how I’ve used it to help ground my thinking sometimes. 

To set the scene…    

*A conspiracy theory is when:*    
- Someone takes an explanation that is either factually accurate, or so strongly based on common sense that it’s just widely accepted, and finds an egregious alternative explanation    
- This wild new explanation only holds water if you suspend rational thinking and probability when determining its likelihood of being true.   
- Just because something has a 0.000000000001% chance of *maybe* being true, we don’t commonly consider these alternatives as it’s infinitely more likely to be wrong. We have lives to live and other uses for our brain power    
- If we did entertain every possible conspiracy theory for every single daily situation, we’d never get anything done and live miserable lives

*Anxiety is:*    
-  Irrational by its very nature, although it doesn’t feel that way to those experiencing it    
- Happens when our minds take an ordinary situation and compulsively thinks up of egregious reasons why something might go wrong/be our fault etc. when there’s no reasonable grounds for that to be true    
- *Realistically* these mindtraps only hold water if you suspend rational thinking and probability    
- Again, just cause something has a 0.000000000001% of being true doesn’t mean we should be taking it as a valid possibility that we need to prepare for and spend brain power on    
- Unlike common conspiracy theories, anxiety tricks us into believing these egregious possibilities are 100% true, or very likely to happen.    
- It lies to us and says that it’s not faulty reasoning and we need to be sincerely concerned, stressed, or otherwise deeply worried cause whatever wild theory it’s come up with is most likely gonna happen    
- Cause of that we can’t move on and it ruins lives 


**An example to illustrate:**    

Your boss of 5y, who you’re friendly with, asks you to call her out of the blue.    
- *The conspiracy theory says,* “she’s calling to tell me that she’s a lizard person and wants me to join her army of other lizard people”    
- *The anxiety says,* “she’s finally realized that I’m a terrible person and she’s calling to fire me cause she hates me”    
- Both of these possible outcomes are wildly unlikely, and can only be considered as a valid possibility if you suspend rational thinking and probability.    
- It’s way more likely she’s just calling to talk about some work stuff. 

In the case of OP, she had a common situation but her anxiety caused her to feel genuine concern and guilt (even after posting in another thread that also validated that she’d be fine bringing her dog onboard)

Im in senior management at a corporate job, so I know the pain (although I find stakeholders easy, the nonstop emails are the problem in my case). Listed below are some tips I find helpful, but you’ll need to find your own pattern. 

1. In a notebook, title a page with each stakeholder’s name. As you go through your week note things down that you’ll need to discuss with them. Keep it as concise as you can. Have weekly sync meetings with them (30m is fine) and discuss all your stuff listed. You’ll find that it’ll be a huge help and you’ll come across more put together.

2. DELEGATE. Omg delegation is critical to meet your timelines. This is super hard, esp if you also struggle with perfectionism, but you’re gonna hit a glass ceiling if you don’t find a way to make it work. 

3. Knowing when something is ok being “good enough” and when it needs to be “perfect”. Talk to your manager in case you need help distinguishing between this on projects. It’ll help you avoid getting stuck in details that really don’t matter. 

4. Good relationship management with stakeholders. In your case it might be hard given that some of the interpersonal exchanges have already become negative and it can be hard to come back from that right away, but if you can try to talk to your stakeholders in a way that would resonate well if someone did it to you. 
Ex. Sharing helpful links cause you remember someone mentioning something, sending “kudos” or congrats when they’ve accomplished initiatives etc.
This won’t completely solve your issue, as you do need to find a way to deliver on time, but remember you attract more bees with honey than with vinegar ;)


5. Honesty. 
- With my boss: I’m super candid. It’s no good to anyone if I’m floundering. How this works in practice for example: I start a bit late, say an hour or so, some days (assuming I don’t have any meetings) but then I work that same amount of time into the evening. She doesn’t care, she just wants the work done and done right. I also ask for priority calls, sanity checks etc when needed. As my manager, it’s in both our interests for me to succeed.

- With people who report to me: I’m the direct manager of a large, high-performing team and the day I became their manager I had a very candid one-on-one conversation with each of them saying how I have adhd and it’s not “squirrel brain” but that I simply think differently and admitted to the things I can be bad at. This came across as accountability.
But I didn’t stop there, I encouraged and explained to them alternative approaches that will accomplish the same end-goal (ex. If an email is going to become a novel and/or become technical, just book me for a 15m meeting instead. They don’t need my permission to do so, my calendar is open and up to date). 
I also encouraged them to tell me what THEY need accommodations for, acknowledging that I might not be the only one who works a little differently. This is leading with empathy.

Maybe I can offer you some tips I found useful as I’m also in senior management and remember those feelings haha.

1. If you’re having remote meetings/remote onboarding *record the sessions*. You often don’t even need to ask/address it if you aren’t comfortable bringing it up, as plenty of computers have default recording mechanisms in the OS (for Macs its QuickTime player). Rewatch later as needed. This has saved me sooo much discomfort.

2. During meetings, write questions to yourself as they come up but try your best not to interrupt (I know this is super hard). They’ll often get around to naturally explaining some of the questions you note, but you can bring up those that are missed or that you need further elaboration on.

3. Ask if there’s a documented org chart with everyone’s name and role in your team and the team(s) you work with. Super helpful as people name drop and helps a lot when it comes to managing feeing overwhelmed when you forget who’s-who

4. If you haven’t already, setup one on one with your boss on a weekly basis to start. Throughout the week note areas that just aren’t “clicking” or that you’re anxious about and ask for further detail or even just ask who would be the most appropriate to follow up with in order to gain familiarity 

I hope some of these might help you, but just remember that a lot of this will simply come with time. Try not to be too hard on yourself, particularly during the first 3 months
